clue.text: Lend dame support, see!

parts.note: to lend is to make a loan; the noun stands in for the verb
a dame holds the DBE, Dame Commander of the Order of the British Empire
to support something is to hold it up

explanation.surface: Someone urges a friend to back a dame with a loan and watch the result.
explanation.walkthrough: DBE is the honour that makes a woman a dame in Britain, so the abbreviation is the letters here.
explanation.definitionFit: The archaic exclamation is used to draw attention to something surprising, just as an imperative 'look!' would.

clue.text: Large snake, I'm afraid, cornering Mike in resort

indicators.note: to corner something is to hem it in, so one word closes round another letter

parts.note: L is the standard size abbreviation for large
an asp is a venomous Egyptian snake
an expression of regret, like the apologetic phrase
Mike is M in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A holiday warning: a big snake has pinned someone called Mike down at the resort.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I'm afraid' is the apologetic sigh, not fear of the snake; it wraps the Mike letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The Canary Islands city is a popular holiday destination, so it qualifies as a seaside resort for tourists.

clue.text: Saw that Tom can spy on Rex?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: an old saying or proverb
second meaning, cryptically: a tom is a male cat and Rex is Latin for king, so a cat may watch a monarch

explanation.surface: Someone notes that Tom is able to keep watch over Rex.
explanation.walkthrough: Saw here is a noun, an old saying, not the past of see; the proverb says even an inferior has some rights in the presence of a superior.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a traditional proverb, and a saw is an old saying or maxim passed down.

clue.text: Maybe take rabbit away from impressionist

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to remove gas, rabbit being slang for chatter or gas, so de-gassing takes it away
second meaning: the French painter of ballet dancers

explanation.surface: A stage impressionist has his rabbit taken away, as if from a conjuring act.
explanation.walkthrough: Rabbit is British slang for idle talk (from rhyming slang rabbit and pork), the same as gas; 'Maybe' flags that de-gas is an invented reading.
explanation.definitionFit: Edgar Degas was a leading painter of the French Impressionist movement, known for ballet scenes.

clue.text: Forte! Is it that of a tattooist?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: very loud, as forte instructs in music

definitions.text: Is it that of a tattooist?
definitions.meaning: second meaning: a service a body-art studio offers alongside tattoos, or the noise of someone beating a drum tattoo

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether a loud flourish is the trademark of a tattoo artist.
explanation.walkthrough: A tattoo is also a drum signal, so a tattooist can be a drummer making a shrill din.
explanation.definitionFit: Forte means loud in musical notation, and a deafeningly loud sound is described as piercing the ears.

clue.text: Possibly topless May Queen, one being pursued

indicators.note: having no top means the word loses its first letter

parts.note: May is one example of a month, as the preceding possibly concedes
ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the royal cipher of the Queen
un is French for one, a common crossword borrowing

explanation.surface: A May Queen, perhaps scantily dressed, is being chased.
explanation.walkthrough: 'May Queen' looks like one festival figure, but May is the month and Queen is separate.
explanation.definitionFit: A fugitive on the run is fleeing pursuers, so the phrase describes someone being chased.

clue.text: Ultimately spineless of French in short ducking a German product

indicators.note: in places these letters inside the following word
cut short means the word loses its last letter

parts.note: a ducking soaks someone thoroughly
taken as written

indicators.note: ultimately points to the final letter of the next word

parts.note: the last letter of spineless
de is French for of

explanation.surface: Something about a feeble Frenchman briefly dodging a German product.
explanation.walkthrough: S and DE go inside DRENCHIN, the ducking word cut short, and A follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Fine porcelain from Meissen near Dresden is known by that city's name, a famous German manufacture.

clue.text: Item for decorating bore inflammatory poster

parts.note: a tiresome person or thing is a pain
an internet troll posts inflammatory comments

explanation.surface: An object for decorating makes a dull, provocative poster.
explanation.walkthrough: Poster is one who posts online, not a printed sheet on a wall.
explanation.definitionFit: A roller with a sleeve is a common tool for applying emulsion to walls when redecorating a room.

clue.text: Flat tyres one can do without!

definitions.meaning: second meaning: someone on foot needs no wheels at all

explanation.walkthrough: 'Flat tyres' reads as a motoring mishap, but Flat is a separate word meaning dull.
explanation.definitionFit: Pedestrian prose is flat and lacking imagination, and a person walking has no need of tyres.

clue.text: American's not always away, we hear, after all

indicators.note: we hear tells us to go by the sound of the phrase rather than its spelling

parts.note: someone who is not always away is in some of the time, an American turn of phrase

explanation.surface: An American who is often absent, we are told, after all.
explanation.walkthrough: Americans say 'some' for 'some of the time', so not always away is 'in some'.
explanation.definitionFit: Both phrases sum up a conclusion: in short, when everything is considered, as after all does.

clue.text: Where council sat to go over ground

parts.note: the Council of Trent met in that Italian city in the 16th century
to bridge a gap is to span or go over it

explanation.surface: A local council met to review the ground.
explanation.walkthrough: TRENT BRIDGE is a Test cricket ground in Nottingham.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a famous sports venue, and a cricket stadium is called a ground in Britain.

clue.text: Trouble and strife, maybe bad for health

indicators.note: bad suggests the letters are spoiled and must be rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Marital trouble and strife are bad for one's health.
explanation.walkthrough: Trouble and strife is Cockney rhyming slang for wife, and 'maybe' marks her as one example.
explanation.definitionFit: A spouse or partner is jokingly called one's better or other half, so a wife is an example.

clue.text: Left one distant land for European city

parts.note: L is the abbreviation for left
the Roman numeral for one
New Zealand, far away from Britain

explanation.surface: An emigrant left a faraway country to settle in a European city.
explanation.definitionFit: Linz is a large city on the Danube in Austria, so it is a European city.

clue.text: Oscar one carried on plate overwhelms film director

indicators.note: to overwhelm is to engulf, so one piece surrounds the other

parts.note: the registration is what a car's number plate carries
Oscar is O in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: An Oscar statuette served on a plate overwhelms a film director at an awards dinner.
explanation.walkthrough: Oscar looks like the film award, apt beside a director, but it is just the letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Nicolas Roeg was the British director of Don't Look Now and Walkabout, so a film director.

clue.text: Second old archbishop's informal words

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for second
Cosmo Lang was Archbishop of Canterbury in the 1930s

explanation.surface: A second elderly archbishop's casual vocabulary.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang is the colloquial vocabulary of everyday speech, a body of casual, non-standard expressions.

clue.text: About time to study alternative to spare tyre?

parts.note: re means concerning or about
T is the abbreviation for time
to read a subject is to study it at university

explanation.surface: It is nearly time to research substitutes for a spare tyre.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits the definition is loose: a remoulded tyre is a cheaper replacement rather than a spare.
explanation.definitionFit: A remoulded tyre with new tread is a budget substitute for buying a brand-new spare wheel.

clue.text: Woman, dismissing daughter, and in hurry to appear on stage

indicators.note: appearing on something means following it, so this piece sits after the next

parts.note: a stage in a process is a step

indicators.note: in places the shortened word inside the next one

parts.note: hie is an old word meaning to hasten

indicators.note: dismissing sends away the named letter from the word it sits in

parts.note: taken as written
D is the abbreviation for daughter

explanation.surface: A mother, leaving her daughter behind, rushes to go on stage.
explanation.walkthrough: Hie is an archaic verb for hurry, still common in crosswords; 'to appear on' puts one piece after another.
explanation.definitionFit: Stephanie is a girl's given name, so it fits a woman in the usual crossword sense.

clue.text: Prepare first off, an end to hostilities

parts.note: to arm is to make ready, especially for battle
1st, with the digit read as the letter I
to off someone and to ice them are both slang for kill

explanation.surface: An instruction to get ready, and first of all, for a ceasefire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First off' reads as 'to begin with', but the two words are separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: An armistice is a formal truce agreed by warring sides, stopping the fighting.

clue.text: Readers of stuff sent out from different dime stores

indicators.note: different means the letters are made into something else

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: People who read items mailed out from various cheap shops.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Readers' suggests people, but these are instruments; stuff sent out is radiation.
explanation.definitionFit: These devices measure the dose of ionising radiation received, so they give readings of emitted energy.

clue.text: Hands-free number?

parts.note: surface reading: a telephone used without holding it
setter's reading: a song admitting a stall has no hands, the bunches in which bananas grow

explanation.walkthrough: A hand is a cluster of bananas, and a number is a song; this is the 1920s novelty song.
explanation.definitionFit: The song's title confesses the grocer is out of bananas, so it is a tune without any hands of fruit.

clue.text: Regulations and data about pick-up from Victoria?

indicators.note: about means going around, so one word wraps the other

parts.note: statistics are data
a ute is an Australian pick-up truck, and Victoria is an Australian state

explanation.surface: Rules and figures about a collection service from London's Victoria station.
explanation.walkthrough: Victoria suggests the London station but is the Australian state, where a ute is the everyday name for a pick-up.
explanation.definitionFit: Statutes are laws passed by a legislature, written rules that govern conduct.

clue.text: Go on board immediately after this cautiously optimistic forecast?

definitions.text: Go on board immediately after this
definitions.meaning: first meaning: the square just before GO on the London Monopoly board
second meaning: read as two words, a guarded weather outlook

explanation.walkthrough: 'Go on board' reads as boarding a ship or plane, but Go is the corner square of the Monopoly board.
explanation.definitionFit: The square in the board game is the last before the GO corner, and as a phrase it predicts possibly good weather.

clue.text: Thrown in debt

definitions.meaning: first meaning: confused, not knowing what to do
second meaning: trading for less than cost

explanation.walkthrough: 'Thrown in debt' reads as one phrase about being plunged into owing money; split, it is two senses.
explanation.definitionFit: Being baffled leaves one bewildered, and a business selling below cost is losing money.

clue.text: Disconcert gunrunner, vetting cases

indicators.note: the words act as cases, holding the solution within their letters

parts.note: the letters run across the two words

explanation.surface: An arms smuggler is unsettled when someone checks his crates.
explanation.walkthrough: Cases looks like packing crates but signals the answer is held inside.
explanation.definitionFit: To unsettle or rattle someone is to disconcert them, robbing them of composure and calm.

clue.text: Cast out to rehearse, expending energy for nothing

indicators.note: expending one thing for another swaps it out, trading the named letter away

parts.note: to practise or drill something
E is the physics symbol for energy
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A director casts out actors so as to practise without wasting effort.
explanation.walkthrough: The second E of the practise word becomes O.
explanation.definitionFit: To exorcise a spirit is to drive it out by ritual, which is to cast it out.

clue.text: For example, a back payment covers substance for lab experiment?

indicators.note: to cover is to go over and enclose, so one word encloses the rest

parts.note: rent is a regular payment for property

indicators.note: back tells us to read the preceding pieces in the opposite direction

parts.note: e.g. abbreviates exempli gratia, for example
taken as written

explanation.surface: A back payment of rent covering the cost of laboratory chemicals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A back payment' reads as arrears, but back goes with EG A.
explanation.definitionFit: A reagent is a chemical added to cause a reaction, used routinely in laboratory tests.

clue.text: Picadors, when thrown, scattered

indicators.note: something thrown lands any old way, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Bullfight horsemen, when tossed by the bull, end up scattered about the ring.
explanation.definitionFit: Sporadic means occurring at irregular intervals or in isolated places, dispersed rather than continuous.

clue.text: What's not faked, unusually, about old Lear's character

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the rearranged letters go round another
unusually means arranged in an unexpected way, so the letters are reordered

parts.note: taken as written
O is the abbreviation for old

explanation.surface: A question about what is genuine in the old King Lear's character.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old Lear' suggests Shakespeare's king, but this is Edward Lear the nonsense poet, whose poem asks 'Who, or why, or which, or what, Is the Akond of Swat?'
explanation.definitionFit: The Akond is the title figure of a nonsense poem by Edward Lear, so one of his comic creations.

clue.text: Singular witticisms, type occurring in yarn

parts.note: S is the grammatical abbreviation for singular
puns are plays on words
ilk means sort or kind

explanation.surface: Odd jokes of a certain kind crop up in a story.
explanation.walkthrough: Yarn suggests a tall tale, but it is thread.
explanation.definitionFit: Spun silk is thread made from short silk fibres twisted together, a kind of yarn for weaving.

clue.text: Butcher's with two floors, one heard

indicators.note: heard means only the sound of this one counts, not its spelling

parts.note: to deck someone is to floor them; this one is spelt as it sounds
a knockout floors a boxer

explanation.surface: A butcher's shop with two storeys, one of them noisy.
explanation.walkthrough: A butcher's is rhyming slang: butcher's hook means look. Floors is a verb twice over, deck and KO.
explanation.definitionFit: Dekko is British slang for a quick look, the same as a butcher's from butcher's hook.

clue.text: Fresh id's one I get ready for computer

indicators.note: fresh means made new, so the letters are reworked

parts.note: taken as written
the Roman numeral for one
taken as written

explanation.surface: A new ID that someone obtains, prepared for use on a computer.
explanation.definitionFit: To digitise is to convert material into a digital form so that computers can process it.

clue.text: Wide crack in which to put leg

indicators.note: putting something in another means one goes inside the other

parts.note: a crack is a joke, and so is a gag
pins is slang for legs

explanation.surface: A big gap that someone might put a leg through.
explanation.walkthrough: Crack wants to mean a gap, which fits the surface; here it means a joke.
explanation.definitionFit: A gaping hole or wound is wide open, so the adjective describes something opened wide.

clue.text: Hides stolen picture from PC, perhaps

parts.note: to screen something is to hide it
hot is slang for stolen goods

explanation.surface: A police officer conceals a stolen photograph.
explanation.walkthrough: PC suggests a police constable, but here it is a personal computer.
explanation.definitionFit: An image captured of a computer display is a screenshot, so a picture taken from a PC.

clue.text: Slip away carrying book, indeed

indicators.note: carrying means holding something within

parts.note: to nod out is to doze off
B is the abbreviation for book

explanation.surface: Someone sneaks off with a book under their arm.
explanation.walkthrough: Slip away suggests leaving the room; here it means drifting off to sleep.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are emphatic agreement words confirming what was said, like certainly or surely.

clue.text: Minister departs, placing inside contact details?

indicators.note: inside means the placing word sits within the minister word

parts.note: a vicar is a minister of the church
to site something is to place it
D is the abbreviation for departs in timetables

explanation.surface: A clergyman leaves after slipping his details into someone's hand.
explanation.definitionFit: A visiting card was left when calling on someone, carrying one's name and address.

clue.text: Come by before safety agency locks garden

parts.note: to come by something is to get it
the Health and Safety Executive, Britain's workplace safety body
a mane is a long head of hair, locks

explanation.surface: Safety inspectors lock up a garden.
explanation.walkthrough: Locks looks like a verb, safety officials padlocking a gate; it is hair.
explanation.definitionFit: Gethsemane is the garden outside Jerusalem where Jesus prayed before his arrest.

clue.text: Old lady embracing English couple overheard Belgian dramatist

indicators.note: to embrace is to hold within one's arms

parts.note: mater is Latin, and old schoolboy slang, for mother
E is the abbreviation for English

indicators.note: overheard means only the spoken sound is needed

parts.note: to couple is to connect

explanation.surface: An elderly woman hugging an English pair heard a Belgian playwright.
explanation.walkthrough: Old lady is a slangy name for one's mother, as is mater.
explanation.definitionFit: Maurice Maeterlinck was the Belgian Nobel-winning author of The Blue Bird and Pelléas and Mélisande.

clue.text: Fifty disembarking from transport to the French African port

indicators.note: disembarking means getting off, so the letter leaves the word

parts.note: transport can mean rapture or ecstasy
L is the Roman numeral for fifty
au is French for to the

explanation.walkthrough: Transport suggests a ship; it is the other sense, being carried away with joy.
explanation.definitionFit: Bissau is the capital and main seaport of Guinea-Bissau in West Africa.

clue.text: Struggling university secretary gets the bird

parts.note: U is the abbreviation for university
a personal assistant does secretarial work
to gain something is to get it
a tit is a small songbird

explanation.surface: A university secretary finds things hard and is shown the door.
explanation.walkthrough: To get the bird is British slang for being booed or dismissed, which suits the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Up against it means facing serious difficulties, so it describes someone who is battling.

clue.text: Parties to hold in a very small Swiss resort

indicators.note: to hold is to have within, so one word surrounds the others

parts.note: dos are parties or social functions
taken as written
small means the word is cut to its abbreviation

explanation.surface: Parties are held in a tiny Swiss resort.
explanation.walkthrough: Small looks like it describes the resort, but it shrinks very to its abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Davos is an Alpine ski town in Switzerland, famous too for the World Economic Forum.

clue.text: Foul slurs wrongly associated with curio

indicators.note: wrongly means put in the incorrect order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Nasty slurs unfairly linked to a collectible trinket.

clue.text: Cap all out of place: the suit and tie back

indicators.note: out of place means the letters are not where they should be

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A cap looks odd: the suit and tie are pulled back.
explanation.walkthrough: Cap is a verb, to outdo.
explanation.definitionFit: To take the biscuit is a British idiom for being the most outrageous of all, so to top or cap everything.

clue.text: Not smart enough to digest page in after-dinner article?

indicators.note: digesting takes something inside, so one word goes into another

parts.note: too thick means too stupid

explanation.surface: Too dim to absorb a page of an article read after a meal.
explanation.walkthrough: Article suggests a piece of writing; it is an object.

clue.text: Tree from US city displayed by sticker book

parts.note: Los Angeles
a bur is a prickly seed case that sticks to clothing
Numbers, the fourth book of the Bible

explanation.surface: A tree from an American city pictured on a book's sticker.
explanation.walkthrough: Sticker looks like a label; it is something that sticks, the bur.
explanation.definitionFit: The laburnum is a small tree with hanging yellow flowers and poisonous seeds.

clue.text: Made up much-loved account — boy's bowled over

explanation.walkthrough: Made up looks like invented, but it means wearing make-up; mascaraed eyelashes are painted.
explanation.definitionFit: Wearing mascara on the eyelashes is one way of being made up with cosmetics.

clue.text: Back from church with claim to devotion — touching!

parts.note: CH is the abbreviation for church
'am pi' is what someone pious claims, pi being slang for pious
on means in contact with

explanation.surface: A moving return from church, with a declaration of faith.
explanation.walkthrough: Back is a verb: to support a cause.
explanation.definitionFit: To champion a cause is to support and defend it, which is what backing it means.

clue.text: A New Jersey sailor visiting centre of Montserrat's capital

indicators.note: a visitor goes into a place, so these letters go inside
the centre of a word is its middle letters

parts.note: the two middle letters of the ten-letter island name
taken as written
the US postal abbreviation for New Jersey
an ordinary seaman

clue.text: Runs course on this country to the west's language

indicators.note: going westward means reading right to left, against the usual direction

a course of a meal is a dish

clue.text: In reducing mistreatment, sorted out public transport

indicators.note: sorted means put into a new order
reducing cuts the word short by its last letter

parts.note: abuse is mistreatment
taken as written

explanation.walkthrough: 'Sorted out' reads as one phrase, but out is part of the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: An autobus is a motor bus, a road vehicle that carries paying passengers on a public route.

clue.text: Winding up following chief, hardly resting

parts.note: CH is an abbreviation for chief

winding up a business is closing it, axing it

clue.text: One who's left note upset timber producer

parts.note: ma is mother
